terms.meaning: the official description of what a valid piece of data looks like.
a rule in the models that rejects bad data when it is created.
a helper that creates a valid example object for tests, so each test only changes what it is testing.
a fixed example input used by tests.
the library used to define the models and check data against them.
a closed list of allowed values, such as the debt types.
the portion of a whole process that one step accounts for, expressed as a fraction.
a score showing how much evidence supports a value, along with what it was based on.

used_by: Test runner (pytest). No other file in the packet calls this file.

sections.name: File setup (part 1)
sections.title: File setup and imports
sections.what: Describes the test style, which is to check specific failure messages rather than only that an error occurred, and brings in the many schema names used by later tests.
sections.why: The header states that a test which only checks for any error keeps passing after the rule it was written for is removed.
sections.watch_out: The file imports many names from the schema package, so removing or renaming one of them breaks the whole file.

sections.name: File setup (part 2)
sections.title: Shared constants and notes on measured features
sections.what: Lists the nine scorecard dimension names and two sets of confidence feature names: one for unmeasured agreement and one for measured agreement.
sections.why: The docstring says fixtures claim agreement was measured, which nothing in the current build actually does.
sections.watch_out: The measured feature set describes a measurement the build does not perform, so it should not be read as evidence that agreement is calculated.

sections.name: step
sections.title: Builder for one process step
sections.what: Creates a valid action step with one share of the process, a duration range, a system, an actor and one evidence id. Options replace any of these.
sections.why: Likely reason: lets tests change only the share or sequence being checked.
sections.watch_out: Shares across several steps must add up to about one, and this builder does not check that for the whole flow.

sections.name: scorecard
sections.title: Builder for a scorecard
sections.what: Creates a scorecard with a score for each of the nine dimensions, each with a rationale and evidence. All scores default to three unless overridden.
sections.why: Likely reason: a neutral middle value gives a valid starting scorecard.
sections.watch_out: The default middle score can hide tests that forgot to set a score they depend on.

sections.name: future_state
sections.title: Builder for a future state design
sections.what: Creates a future state with one designed agent, one step performed by that agent, an exception model with an escalation trigger and a response time, a moderate posture and one evidence id.
sections.why: Likely reason: a complete valid design so tests can change one part.
sections.watch_out: The agent and step names must match each other, so renaming one without the other breaks the builder.

sections.name: value_parameters
sections.title: Builder for value parameters
sections.what: Creates value ranges for effort, automation, assistance, cycle time, error rate and adoption ramp, plus one shared enabler and one prerequisite.
sections.why: Likely reason: a complete valid set of inputs for the value-related tests.
sections.watch_out: The values are invented fixtures and are not tied to any real process.

sections.name: confidence
sections.title: Builder for one confidence record
sections.what: Creates a confidence record with a score, four evidence items, a source age, source agreement of 0.8 and the measured feature list.
sections.why: The docstring explains it marks agreement as measured so the consistency rules are satisfied.
sections.watch_out: The agreement value is a made-up number, not a real measurement.

sections.name: all_block_confidence
sections.title: Builder for a confidence record per block
sections.what: Creates one confidence record for each of the six block names, using 0.6 by default and any override supplied by block name.
sections.why: Likely reason: a process record needs one confidence entry per block.

sections.name: feasibility
sections.title: Builder for feasibility assessment
sections.what: Creates one safety constraint that requires a human to decide, a data readiness record with one dataset, and a binding autonomy ceiling of human decides.
sections.why: The docstring says one named constraint makes the binding ceiling a real value rather than the empty default.
sections.watch_out: The example uses a specific jurisdiction and requirement, so tests depending on them need that wording kept.

sections.name: record (part 1)
sections.title: Builder for a full process record (first part)
sections.what: Starts a complete valid process record, filling in identity, description, work unit, annual volume, current state with steps, pain points and workflow debt, and a scorecard.
sections.why: Likely reason: most tests need a complete valid record, so one shared builder keeps them consistent.
sections.watch_out: Because most tests depend on this builder, a new required field in the record breaks many tests at once.

sections.name: record (part 2)
sections.title: Builder for a full process record (completion)
sections.what: Adds the remaining parts to the record, including future state, implications, feasibility, value parameters, confidence per block, challenges and a fresh run id, then creates the record with any overrides applied.
sections.why: Likely reason: keeps every block valid so tests change only the part they check.
sections.watch_out: A fresh run id is created on every call, so two records built this way are never equal.

sections.name: messages
sections.title: Helper for reading error messages
sections.what: Returns the text of a validation error so tests can check its wording.
sections.why: Likely reason: keeps the assertions short.
sections.watch_out: Tests depend on the exact wording, so changing the message text breaks them.

sections.name: TestRange
sections.title: Range rules
sections.what: Checks that low, base and high must be in order, that a range has a width, that a range with zero width is legal, that a range cannot be changed after creation, and that unknown fields such as currency are rejected.
sections.why: Reason not stated in the code beyond the ordering rule and the examples given in the messages.
sections.watch_out: The tests check exact message text that includes the offending value, so message changes break them.

sections.name: TestNonNegativeRange
sections.title: Non-negative range rule
sections.what: Accepts a zero low value and rejects a negative low value.
sections.why: Reason not stated in the code. It is likely there because the range is used for effort or durations that cannot be negative.

sections.name: TestUnitRange
sections.title: Unit range rules (zero to one)
sections.what: Accepts ranges within zero to one, rejects values above one or below zero, and checks that ordering still applies.
sections.why: Reason not stated in the code. It is likely there because these ranges are shares or rates.

sections.name: TestClosedVocabularies
sections.title: Closed lists of allowed values
sections.what: Checks that the debt types are exactly the twelve listed, that an unknown debt type is rejected with a message listing the valid ones, that an unknown enabler id is rejected, and that the six block names are exactly those expected.
sections.why: Reason not stated in the code beyond keeping the valid values fixed and visible in messages.
sections.watch_out: Adding a debt type or block name requires updating these lists deliberately.

sections.name: TestCurrentState (part 1)
sections.title: Step shares, warnings and references
sections.what: Shares that add to about one raise no warning, small drift within tolerance raises no warning, and larger drift raises a warning with the actual sum rather than an error. Duplicate step numbers and pain points that point to missing steps are rejected.
sections.why: Reason not stated in the code for the warning instead of an error. The docstrings suggest drift is a data quality issue, not a reason to stop.
sections.watch_out: Drift only warns and does not block. Any caller that turns warnings into errors will stop on normal drift.

sections.name: TestCurrentState: test_workflow_debt_referencing_a_missing_step_is_rejected
sections.title: Workflow debt and step limits
sections.what: Workflow debt that points to missing steps is rejected. A single step share above one is rejected. Severity must be from one to five.
sections.why: Reason not stated in the code beyond keeping references valid and values in range.
sections.watch_out: Severity limits are written into the test, so a new scale needs both the model and this test changed.

sections.name: TestScorecard
sections.title: Checking the scorecard fields and scores
sections.what: Checks that the scorecard has all nine dimensions, that each score is a whole number from 0 to 5, that every rationale has text, and that the two inverted dimensions are labelled as such in their descriptions while the others say higher is better.
sections.why: Reason not stated in the code for the exact range, though the test names show that scores are meant to be comparable across dimensions. Inverted dimensions are the ones where a high number is bad, so their labels stop a reader reading them the wrong way.
sections.watch_out: If a dimension changes direction, its description text and the inverted list must both change, or these tests disagree with reality.

sections.name: TestFutureState (part 1)
sections.title: Future-state steps and agent rules
sections.what: Checks that a future-state step done by a designed agent must name an agent that is in the agent list, that step numbers and agent names are unique, and that the exception model is required. A step done by a human does not need a matching agent.
sections.why: Stops a future-state design from pointing at agents that were never defined. Human steps are exempt on purpose, as the test name says.
sections.watch_out: The human exemption is deliberate. Do not tighten the agent check to cover every step without thinking about human steps.

sections.name: TestFutureState: test_unlisted_posture_is_rejected
sections.title: Unknown posture is refused
sections.what: Checks that a posture value outside the allowed list, here an invented word, is refused and the error names the allowed options.
sections.why: Keeps the posture to a fixed set of words that other parts of the system can compare.
sections.watch_out: The allowed list lives in the schema. Adding or renaming a posture means updating this test's expectations.

sections.name: TestValueParameters
sections.title: Value parameters and shares
sections.what: Checks that the automatable and assisted shares cannot add to more than full coverage at their upper bounds, that no money or total fields exist, that a smuggled total is rejected, that every estimated parameter is a range, and that prerequisite kinds come from a closed list.
sections.why: Keeps value estimates as ranges and stops totals from being stored, which matches the rule that the schema holds no money. Reason for the share limit is stated in the error message: work cannot be more than fully covered.
sections.watch_out: The share check uses upper bounds. Loosening those bounds would let two shares overlap without any error.

sections.name: TestConfidence
sections.title: Confidence score rules
sections.what: Checks that a confidence score sits between 0 and 1, that evidence counts cannot be negative, that the method defaults to computed and that any other method is refused. It also checks that zero evidence with a zero score is the one legal way to record no support.
sections.why: A confidence number is only meaningful if it came from counted evidence. Zero evidence with zero score is how the system states that a block is unsupported.
sections.watch_out: The accepted method list has to match what the code actually writes, or valid records will be refused.

sections.name: TestChallenge
sections.title: Challenge records cannot set confidence
sections.what: Checks that a challenge record has no confidence or score field, that upheld defaults to false, and that a challenge against an unknown block is refused.
sections.why: A challenger should object to a claim but not assign its own confidence number. Reason beyond this is not stated in the code.
sections.watch_out: The list of valid blocks must stay in step with the schema, or challenges against real blocks will be wrongly refused.

sections.name: TestProcessRecord
sections.title: Process record behaviour
sections.what: Checks that a complete record validates, that the schema version defaults to the current constant, that a record missing any confidence block is refused and names the gap, that record-level confidence is the lowest block score rather than the average, that records cannot be changed after creation, that a smuggled currency field is refused, and that records survive a JSON round trip unchanged.
sections.why: Taking the minimum means one weak block lowers the whole record, so a strong block cannot hide a weak one. The test names say this was a deliberate choice.
sections.watch_out: The minimum rule is what protects against a strong block hiding a weak one. Changing it to an average would quietly weaken the record.

sections.name: TestNoMoneyAnywhereInTheSchema (part 1)
sections.title: Finding every schema model
sections.what: Sets up a helper that finds every data model in the schema package, including modules the package does not publicly export, and checks that the case input models are among them.
sections.why: An earlier version of the money check only looked at publicly exported models, so a model in a hidden module escaped it. The comments say this was fixed.
sections.watch_out: The helper attaches models to the package as a side effect. A change to how the package is imported could change what it finds.

sections.name: TestNoMoneyAnywhereInTheSchema: test_no_model_in_the_contract_declares_a_money_field
sections.title: No money fields in the contract
sections.what: Checks that no data model in the schema has a field with a money-like name, such as cost, savings or total, except two named exemptions. It also checks that the view agents see has no money fields.
sections.why: The spec says the schema holds no currency. The two exemptions, the run manifest and the client context, are written down as decisions with reasons in the code comments.
sections.watch_out: Each new exemption is a gap in the rule. Adding one without a stated reason would quietly weaken the guard.

sections.name: TestEvidenceLinkageIsRequired (part 1)
sections.title: Evidence links are required
sections.what: Checks that each listed evidence field is required both on its model and in the exported JSON schema, and that a step without evidence is refused.
sections.why: A missing field and an empty list mean different things. A default on these fields would let a model skip citing evidence, and the exported schema is what the model is shaped by.
sections.watch_out: Adding a default to any listed field will fail these tests on purpose. That is the intended protection, not a bug.

sections.name: TestEvidenceLinkageIsRequired: test_explicit_empty_evidence_is_still_legal
sections.title: Explicit empty evidence is allowed
sections.what: Checks that an evidence list stated as empty is accepted, for a step, a shared enabler list, and value parameters. This records a deliberate choice that nothing supports the claim.
sections.why: Recording an unsupported hypothesis honestly must be possible. The test's own comment says so.
sections.watch_out: This is the counterpart of the required-field tests in the previous section. Merging the two into one rule would break either the honesty or the strictness.

sections.name: TestConfidenceCannotBeFabricated
sections.title: Confidence cannot be made up
sections.what: Checks that a confidence block with zero evidence cannot carry a positive score, that the zero-evidence zero-score case is accepted, that evidence-backed confidence is unaffected, and that a full record cannot hide a fake block score.
sections.why: A score with no evidence behind it would look computed. The comments say the method field alone only stopped a model naming a different source, so this rule is what stops invented numbers.
sections.watch_out: This zero-evidence rule is the main protection against invented confidence numbers. Relaxing it would reopen that gap.

sections.name: TestPatternIdSharesTheEnablerVocabulary
sections.title: Pattern ids come from the shared list
sections.what: Checks that a designed agent's pattern id must come from the shared enabler list and free text is refused. It also checks that having no pattern is allowed and that the pattern field and shared enabler field draw on the same list.
sections.why: Both fields must use one vocabulary so that duplicates can be matched. The comments say the two must stay joinable.
sections.watch_out: A new enabler has to be added to the one shared list, or it cannot be recorded in either field.

sections.name: TestSchemaVersionIsCarriedNotAssumed
sections.title: Schema version must be stated
sections.what: Checks that the schema version is required, that a payload with no version is refused, that unknown or nonsense versions are refused with the current version named, and that the current version is in the list of known versions.
sections.why: A default version would silently call old data current. The comments describe this as a past finding.
sections.watch_out: When the version constant is bumped, the known-versions list must be updated too, or current records will be refused.

sections.name: TestInvertedDimensionsConstantTracksTheScorecard
sections.title: Inverted dimension list matches scorecard
sections.what: Checks that every dimension named as inverted is a real field on the scorecard.
sections.why: Stops a typo or removed field in the inverted list from going unnoticed.
sections.watch_out: This only checks that the named fields exist. It does not check that the right dimensions are in the list.

sections.name: TestTheFeatureAccountCannotDisagreeWithItself (part 1)
sections.title: Feature account rules and setup
sections.what: Sets up a helper with a valid confidence payload and checks that valid measured and unmeasured shapes are accepted. It also checks that declaring agreement without a value is refused, and that a stored agreement value without a declaration is refused.
sections.why: The feature list is the audit trail for a confidence score, so it must agree with the stored values. The control test makes sure the other checks are not passing just because everything is rejected.
sections.watch_out: The helper's payload must stay in step with the model fields, or every test in this group fails for the wrong reason.

sections.name: TestTheFeatureAccountCannotDisagreeWithItself: test_an_always_computable_feature_must_be_declared
sections.title: Coverage and recency must be declared
sections.what: Checks that a feature list missing coverage or recency is refused, and that an invented feature name is refused.
sections.why: Coverage and recency always apply, so a record that omits them describes a score the formula cannot produce.
sections.watch_out: The list of always-computed features must match the formula. Changing the formula without this list will cause false passes or false failures.

sections.name: TestTheScoreIsReproducibleFromWhatIsStored (part 1)
sections.title: Recomputing a score from stored fields
sections.what: Sets up a helper that recomputes a confidence score using only the stored fields, then checks that every block of a computed record reproduces its score and that the recomputation matches across a grid of citation and gap counts.
sections.why: The stated goal is that an auditor with only the record can recalculate the number. The helper reads the declared features, so a missing agreement value is treated as absent rather than as a real measurement.
sections.watch_out: The helper copies the published formula. If the formula changes in the code, this helper must change too, or the tests will fail or, worse, pass against a stale copy.

sections.name: TestTheScoreIsReproducibleFromWhatIsStored: test_the_two_situations_no_longer_collide
sections.title: Thin and hollow evidence stay distinct
sections.what: Checks that two citations and five citations resting on three gaps store different counts even though their effective coverage is the same. It also checks that gaps larger than citations give an effective count of zero and a score of zero, and that a positive score with all evidence cancelled is refused.
sections.why: A reader must be able to tell thin evidence from well-cited work built on assumptions. The comments say netting the gaps into the count made these look the same.
sections.watch_out: The effective count is citations minus gaps, floored at zero. Storing the netted number instead of the raw count would bring back the collision.

sections.name: TestTheFeatureVocabularyIsSingleSourced
sections.title: Feature names have one source
sections.what: Checks that the feature order list and the feature name type list the same names, that the always-measurable features are in the order list, and that the agreement minimum is two in both the schema and the knowledge package.
sections.why: The comments record that a feature missing from the order list was silently dropped. Keeping one source avoids that.
sections.watch_out: Adding a feature name to only one of the two places causes either silent loss or a name that can never be stored.

sections.name: TestTheFeatureAccountIsCanonicalised (part 1)
sections.title: Feature lists are put in one order
sections.what: Checks that feature lists in any order, with or without duplicates, are stored as one standard order, so that equal records produce identical output bytes.
sections.why: Replays are compared byte for byte, and the comments say the checkpoint store relies on this. Equality alone is not enough because the serialised text must also match.
sections.watch_out: Changing the standard order changes what gets stored. Any saved record that relied on the old order will no longer match byte for byte.

sections.name: TestTheFeatureAccountIsCanonicalised: test_a_measured_block_canonicalises_with_agreement_last
sections.title: Agreement goes last and nothing is dropped
sections.what: Checks that a measured block puts agreement last in its feature list, that a name outside the type is refused by the type check, and that a feature missing from the order list is refused rather than silently removed. A counterfactual check shows that the silent-removal version would return a shorter list.
sections.why: Silent removal would hide which features produced a score. The comments say the refusal is a backstop in case the type check is ever bypassed.
sections.watch_out: Every feature name must appear in the order list. A new feature missing from it is refused, which is intended but will surprise someone adding a feature.

sections.name: TestTheThinnessRuleIsInTheContract
sections.title: Thinness rule for measured agreement
sections.what: Checks that a measured agreement needs at least two effective citations. One citation, zero citations, or a well-cited block whose gaps bring it below two are all refused. An unmeasured block is not affected.
sections.why: Agreement between one source is not meaningful. The rule counts effective evidence, not raw citations, so the gaps are part of the check.
sections.watch_out: Any check on this rule must use the effective count after gaps, not the raw citation count, or gap-heavy blocks will get through.

summary: The main contract test file for the schema package, checking the shape, limits, vocabularies and consistency rules of the process record and its parts. Only the first 499 of 1475 lines were shown in this packet.
purpose: Protects the data model that every stage of the pipeline reads and writes, so bad values are rejected at creation rather than causing silent errors later.
why: The header says every validator needs a test, and each rejection test must check the specific failure rather than just that something failed, so a test cannot keep passing after its rule is removed.
how: Builder helpers create valid examples, and each test changes one thing and checks the error or the warning. Grouped classes cover ranges, vocabularies, current state, scorecard and later parts.
inputs: The schema models imported from packages/schema, plus hand-made fixtures built in this file.
outputs: Pass or fail results. Some tests also check that a warning is raised.
risks: Most tests build a full process record, so a new required field in the record breaks many tests at once. Many checks depend on exact error wording. Fixtures use invented values, so they show intent rather than real data.
debug: Start with the failing test name, which names the rule. Read the message in the assertion, then find that rule in packages/schema. If many tests fail together, check the shared record builder first. If only a warning test fails, check the share sum tolerance in the schema.
